title: Anas Al-Sharif One Year Later: The Systematic Killing of Palestine’s Journalists
author: Michael Leonardi
content:

One year ago this week, the Israeli military killed Anas Al-Sharif. He was a
young Palestinian journalist working in Gaza, one of the many who continued to
report under bombardment, displacement, and the constant knowledge that the
camera itself had become a target. His death was not an accident of war. It
was one act in the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza — a
genocide that has included, as a deliberate and central component, the
systematic elimination of those who document it.

Al-Sharif’s killing joins a list that has grown so long it has become a
statistic rather than a series of individual lives. Since October 2023, more
close to three hundred Palestinian and now Lebanese journalists and media
workers have been killed by Israeli forces. The Committee to Protect
Journalists documents at least 209 killed by Israel in Gaza and in Israeli
detention centres. Palestinian press associations and the International
Federation of Journalists put the figure higher, in the mid-to-high 260s.
These were not combatants. They were reporters, camera operators, producers,
and fixers — many of them wearing clearly marked press vests, working for
local outlets or international networks, trying to show the world what was
happening to their cities, their schools, their mosques, their hospitals, and
their families as the genocide unfolded.

This is not merely the deadliest conflict for journalists in the modern era.
According to analyses from Brown University’s Costs of War project, more
journalists have been killed in Gaza than in the U.S. Civil War, World War I,
World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War (including Cambodia and Laos),
the wars in the former Yugoslavia, and the post-9/11 war in Afghanistan —
combined. The comparison is not rhetorical flourish. It is a measure of the
scale of a genocidal campaign that has treated the press as an enemy to be
erased. What took place across the major industrial wars of the twentieth
century, across continents and decades, has been surpassed in a single strip
of land in less than three years. That fact alone should end any pretence that
these deaths are the ordinary hazards of covering combat.

Among the dead is Shireen Abu Akleh, the American-Palestinian journalist for
Al Jazeera, shot in the head by an Israeli soldier in Jenin in May 2022 — more
than a year before the onset of the current genocide in Gaza. She was wearing
a helmet and a press vest while covering a military raid. Her killing was
captured on video. Investigations by independent outlets and human rights
organizations concluded that she was deliberately targeted. The Israeli
government first claimed she was killed by Palestinian fire, then shifted
stories, and ultimately faced no meaningful accountability. Her targeted
killing was an early and clear signal of the policy that would later be
applied on a mass scale as part of the genocide: the press is the enemy.

The pattern is consistent with the logic of genocide. Journalists are killed
in their homes with their families, in marked press cars, while live-streaming
from hospital courtyards, while sheltering in media offices that Israeli
officials had been informed were civilian. Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau was
repeatedly struck. Local reporters who remained after international staff were
evacuated became the primary chroniclers of the mass killing, the destruction
of civilian infrastructure, and the forced starvation of the population — and
therefore the primary targets. Israel’s repeated claim that it does not target
journalists is contradicted by the body count, by the documented strikes on
known media locations, and by the statements of Israeli officials who have
treated the Palestinian press as a legitimate military objective within a
broader campaign of destruction.

Yet some have survived the same violence and refused to stop. Wael Al-Dahdouh,
Al Jazeera’s long-time Gaza bureau chief, lost his wife, two of his children,
his infant grandson, and later his eldest son Hamza — himself a journalist —
in successive Israeli strikes. He was injured more than once. Within days of
burying family members he returned to the camera. “If we don’t continue
reporting,” he has said, “there will be no one left to tell the story.” Even
after leaving Gaza for medical treatment, he has continued to speak for the
colleagues still inside. Others who narrowly escaped the August 2025 strike
that killed Anas Al-Sharif and four of his colleagues — among them Ayman al-
Hassi, Mohammed Qita, and Anas’s cousin Mohammed al-Sharif — returned to the
same work. Younger reporters such as Nour Khaled stepped into the gap left by
the dead, choosing to remain in Gaza City rather than evacuate, insisting that
the coverage must continue.

These survivors operate under conditions that would be unimaginable in any
other context: no safe shelter, no reliable electricity, chronic hunger, and
the knowledge that the next airstrike may be aimed at them specifically.
Freelancers without institutional protection, local stringers, and the
remaining staff of networks that still broadcast from Gaza keep documenting
the genocide because no one else can. Their persistence is itself a form of
resistance against the attempt to erase the record.

This is a genocidal attack on freedom of the press, inseparable from the
genocide itself. When a state kills the people who record its actions at a
rate that exceeds the combined toll of the great wars of the twentieth
century, it is not simply committing war crimes against individuals. It is
attempting to erase the possibility of an independent historical record of the
genocide. The images that did get out — of children pulled from rubble, of
mass graves, of hospitals turned into morgues — were produced at extraordinary
personal cost. Many of the journalists who filmed them are now dead. Those who
remain keep working.

The names of those killed are not abstract. They are maintained and updated by
Palestinian institutions themselves. The Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate
(نقابة الصحفيين الفلسطينيين), working in close coordination with the
International Federation of Journalists, has published sequential lists of the
martyred journalists and media workers. A public, regularly updated record of
the killings can be found on the IFJ’s dedicated page for the war in Gaza,
which draws directly from the Syndicate’s documentation. Additional named
lists and ongoing monitoring are available through the Shireen Observatory
(مرصد شيرين) at <https://www.shireen.ps>, a Palestinian project dedicated to
documenting attacks on journalists. These are the primary Palestinian sources
for the identities of those silenced.

Last week in New York City, like in many places across the world,
demonstrators marked the one-year anniversary of Anas Al-Sharif’s killing.
Organized in part by the Palestinian Youth Movement, the march moved from the
New York Times building to Times Square, demanding accountability for the
journalists killed in Gaza and spotlighting Western media’s role in
manufacturing consent for the ongoing genocide. Among those present was
Palestinian American activist Roland Bennett, president of the Tree Water
Initiative, a non profit dedicated to supporting sustainable life in Gaza.
“Remembering Anas means refusing to let the record be buried,” Bennet said.
“Every journalist still reporting from Gaza is carrying the weight of those
who can no longer speak. Our task is to make sure the world cannot look away.”

The international response has been a mixture of muted statements and
continued arms transfers. Western governments that speak of press freedom at
home have remained largely silent about the industrial-scale killing of
Palestinian journalists as part of the genocide. The same governments that
demanded accountability when journalists were killed in Ukraine have found
reasons for caution when the perpetrators are their close ally. The double
standard is not subtle. It is structural.

Anas Al-Sharif was one name among hundreds. His colleagues continue to report
from the ruins. Their work is an act of resistance against both the genocide
itself and the attempt to erase its documentation. One year after his death,
the least that can be demanded is that the record remain unbroken: these
killings were not tragic accidents of a complex war. They were the systematic
targeting of the people who refused to look away — a campaign so extensive
that it has outstripped the journalist death tolls of World War I, World War
II, and the major conflicts of the modern era combined, and one that forms an
integral part of the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

The silence of the powerful is part of the crime. The work of the remaining
journalists who seek to expose the truth is its contradiction and a part of
the resistance to these unfathomable and ongoing atrocities continuing to
happen before our eyes.
